landing.metaTitle: ReproSense: a cycle record her doctor can read in a minute
landing.eyebrow: For women in Abu Dhabi · private · free
landing.h1: Bring your doctor a year of cycles, not a memory.
landing.lede: ReproSense turns a woman's period logs, pain scores and lab reports into a record her gynaecologist can read in a minute. It points out patterns worth checking, shows the entries behind each one, and never diagnoses.
landing.who: Free for women. For women's health and IVF clinics, a subscription that closes missed follow-ups. Built for the HealthX Ajyal Hackathon, Department of Health – Abu Dhabi.

landing.evidenceTitle: The history exists. It arrives at the appointment in pieces.
landing.ev1: Up to 70% of women with PCOS are not aware of it, the World Health Organization estimates. In the UAE Healthy Future Study, 25.9% of 1,040 Emirati women aged 25 to 67 reported PCOS; in one Dubai hospital's records, it was coded for 1.6% of women aged 15 to 45. The two studies count different groups in different ways.
landing.ev2: Endometriosis takes years to name. Across 23 studies worldwide, the average delay from first symptoms was 6.8 years. In a UAE study of 518 women with confirmed endometriosis, it was 11.6 years.
landing.ev3: About 1 in 5 pregnancies in Al Ain's Mutaba'ah study had gestational diabetes (21.3%). After the birth, the glucose test that catches type 2 diabetes early is easy to miss: at one Al Ain hospital (2013–14 data), only 265 of 1,043 women who had gestational diabetes (25.4%) came back for it.
landing.ev4: Abu Dhabi is already moving: in September 2026 the Department of Health launched its Programme for the Future of Reproductive Health, built on prevention and early screening, with a goal of raising IVF success from 59% to 80% by 2030.
landing.traceTitle: Follow one observation from her phone to the clinic.
landing.traceIntro: Rules decide, published guidelines ground, and the language model only explains. This is Noura's path through the system, using her fictional data.
landing.t1Title: She logs in about twenty seconds
landing.t1Body: {days} days logged over 12 months: flow, pain, symptoms and a bleeding score.
landing.t2Body: {outside} of her last {count} cycles were outside 21–35 days, so the irregular-cycles rule fires. No AI makes this decision.
landing.t3Body: The card cites the 2023 International PCOS Guideline and lists the entries behind it.
landing.t4Body: With her consent, the clinic sees a handover summary and closes follow-ups.
landing.modelTitle: Two people use it. One pays.
landing.womenBody: Logging takes about twenty seconds: flow, pain from 0 to 10, a bleeding score using the same pictorial chart gynaecologists use, or a sentence in Arabic or English. She sees her year on one screen, gets questions to ask, and decides who sees her report and for how long.

landing.clinicBody: Before the visit the clinician receives a structured history in a standard handover format, the evidence behind each pattern, and extracted lab values. The clinic dashboard lists follow-ups that are due, such as glucose tests after gestational diabetes, and shows them closing.
landing.clinicPrice: From AED 399 per clinician per month, a hypothesis we are testing in clinic interviews.

trust.title: Trust centre
trust.intro: How ReproSense answers the Department of Health's Responsible AI Standard, clause by clause, and what it does not claim. Each clause is summarised in our own words.

r1.asks: Design with clinicians and patients, and fit the clinic's workflow.
r1.ours: The clinician view follows a visit: a one-minute summary, the evidence for each line and a visit-note draft she edits. A clinical advisor and pilot clinicians will review it.

r2.asks: Keep a human in or on the loop, with escalation by risk.
r2.ours: Clinicians decide. The care navigator only drafts, and she approves every message; nothing is sent on its own. Red flags come first with 998, and a self-harm answer in the mood check opens the crisis path.

r3.asks: Fail safely, with a fallback, and monitor after launch.
r3.ours: Without a language model, every card keeps fixed template wording and the assistant quotes the knowledge base. 3D views fall back to static pictures. Monitoring after launch comes with the pilot.

r4.asks: Validate against benchmarks and keep the results.
r4.ours: A fixed test set runs on every change: grounded answers, refused diagnosis questions, red-flag recall and banned phrases. The latest results are on the team scorecard.

r5.asks: Role-based access, least privilege, and every access logged.
r5.ours: Patient, clinician and network-admin roles are separate, and the database enforces them with row-level security. Every view of her record goes into a tamper-evident audit log that she can read. Multi-factor sign-in is planned.

r6.asks: Privacy by design: minimum data, encryption, no training on patient data.
r6.ours: Records use a nickname, not a name. Notes and documents are encrypted (AES-256-GCM). Model calls receive de-identified text only, and no model is trained on her data.

r7.asks: Compute and storage, disaster recovery included, inside the UAE.
r7.ours: This demo holds fictional data only. Production will run on UAE-region cloud with disaster recovery in the UAE, a UAE-hosted model or no model, and support access from inside the UAE.

r8.asks: Data that reflects the population, with gaps between groups checked.
r8.ours: The network dashboard compares flagged and sharing rates by nationality group and age band, marks gaps over 5 points and hides groups under 10 women. A data card for the synthetic data is planned.

r9.asks: Tell people when AI is used, and let patients opt out.
r9.ours: The footer says AI tools are used, and every card says how it was written. Her Privacy switch turns AI off: the assistant closes and no text of hers reaches a model. New records start with AI off.

r10.asks: Document sources, logic and decision criteria; log inputs, outputs and versions.
r10.ours: Observation rules live in one versioned file, each with its guideline source. Every card shows the entries and the rule behind it, with a step-by-step trace of how it was produced.

r11.asks: Explain in a way that fits each role.
r11.ours: She reads plain language and questions for her doctor. Her clinician reads a short handover with the evidence for each line. No card shows a probability.

r12.asks: Named owners, and clinicians keep final authority, with an audit trail.
r12.ours: Clinicians edit the visit note and book or close each follow-up, and each action is logged. Named owners will be set in the pilot agreement.

r13.asks: Keep a risk register; high-risk systems need a DoH conformity assessment.
r13.ours: ReproSense is designed to inform, never to diagnose, which supports a lower risk tier. A risk register will be written before the pilot.

not.n1: ReproSense does not diagnose. It points out patterns worth discussing with a doctor.
not.n2: It is checked against a fixed test set, not clinically validated. We quote no accuracy figure.
not.n3: Whether it is a medical device is for the regulator to decide. We will ask the Emirates Drug Establishment before any pilot.
not.n4: Every record in this demo is fictional.
not.n5: UAE hosting, the ADHICS assessment and a clinician's sign-off on the rules are next steps, not done.
not.n6: We never describe it as early detection, screening for PCOS, a risk score, fertile or safe days, or an AI doctor.

trust.data1: She decides who sees her record: sharing with a clinic is a separate choice she can stop at any time, and the clinic loses access at once.
trust.data2: She can read who viewed her record, download everything (including a FHIR R4 export for her clinic's system) and delete her entries.
trust.data3: We never sell health data or show ads.
trust.sourceDoh: Department of Health Abu Dhabi, Responsible AI Standard, version 1 (October 2025)
trust.seePrivacy: Try the privacy centre as Noura
trust.intendedBody: ReproSense is a personal health record and consultation-preparation tool. A woman records her own cycles, symptoms, questionnaires and lab results. ReproSense organises them, shows where her entries meet published guideline thresholds that are worth discussing, and creates a summary she can choose to share with her clinic. It does not diagnose, treat, predict or prevent disease, does not give contraceptive advice, and does not replace a clinician's judgement. Clinicians see the entries and the guideline behind every item.
trust.data4: In this demo, deleting removes your entries at once. UAE law asks health records to be kept for 25 years, so before any real data we will agree with the Department of Health how deletion and that rule work together.
